chapters.blurb: Age sets the prior before a symptom is mentioned

skill.particulars.demographics.expect: Expect disease after middle age: most carcinomas present past forty, and rectal bleeding in an older adult carries a far higher prior than identical bleeding in a young adult. Late presentation from rural practice is common, so never let a long history of piles reassure you without examination.

chapters.title: Patient particulars

chapters.blurb: Months, not days, with bleeding that has a relation to stool

skill.hx.chief_complaints.expect: Expect a story told in months: bleeding per rectum for months, gradually altered bowel habit, then weight loss and tiredness. That slow tempo separates colorectal cancer from an acute infective diarrhoea or a painful anal emergency measured in days.

skill.hx.surg.rectal_bleeding_pain.expect: In this disease expect painless bleeding mixed with mucus rather than the painful bright streak of a fissure or the painless splash of piles. Ask how blood relates to stool: mixed with faeces points above the sigmoid, coating the surface points to rectum or anal canal, and blood with mucus passed separately fits an ulcerated rectal growth.

chapters.title: History of presenting illness

chapters.blurb: The risk factors that raise the prior and the fitness that allows the operation
chapters.title: Past, personal, drug and family history

chapters.blurb: Pallor and weight loss outrank the abdomen

skill.gen.appearance.expect: Look for pallor of chronic blood loss with recent weight loss and tiredness, sometimes with ankle swelling from low protein in advanced disease. A right sided growth can look like nothing more than a tired anaemic adult until the bowel is examined.

skill.gen.vitals.expect: Vitals are usually normal in uncomplicated disease. Tachycardia with postural symptoms reflects anaemia; fever, tachycardia and hypotension mean obstruction with sepsis or perforation and change the urgency entirely.

chapters.title: General examination

chapters.blurb: The finger, the scope, the lump and the nodes

skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.expect: Expect blood stained mucus on the verge or staining of clothes, sometimes with excoriation from discharge. Piles or a sentinel pile may coexist and mislead: a visible pile never excuses omitting the digital examination.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.expect: This is the examination that makes the diagnosis: an ulcerated growth with a raised everted edge and indurated base, often on the anterior wall within reach of the finger. Record distance from the verge, clock position, circumference involved, mobility on the muscle, and whether the glove carries blood or mucus.

skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.expect: Expect to see the growth directly: a friable ulcerated or proliferative mass that bleeds on contact, with normal mucosa above it. Proctoscopy also lets you biopsy, which is the point of passing the instrument.

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.expect: Expect either no abdominal lump, with a loaded descending colon that pits on pressure above an annular rectal lesion, or a firm mass in the right iliac fossa in caecal growths. A hard nodular liver edge or ascites means distant spread and changes operability.

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.expect: Palpate the groins: growths at or below the dentate line can spread to inguinal nodes, while higher rectal and colonic growths drain to pelvic nodes beyond the hand. A hard left supraclavicular node hints at distant spread and inoperability.

fullName: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum
name: Carcinoma colon and rectum
oneLine: Altered bowel habit with rectal bleeding, and the rectal examination and staging that decide the operation

skill.reasoning.colorectal.basics.oneLine: One name for three diseases divided by site: right, left and rectal
pitfalls: Calling every rectal bleed piles without ever placing the lesion above or below the sigmoid.
Treating a right sided anaemia and a rectal tenesmus as one presentation instead of opposite ends of the colon.
Forgetting the adenoma sequence, so polyps are ignored and family screening is never offered.
Assuming a negative stool blood test excludes cancer, when half of proven cancers bleed intermittently.

probes.a: Most colorectal cancers develop from adenomatous polyps through accumulating genetic changes, with villous adenomas progressing about three times as often as tubular ones.
probes.q: Where do most colorectal cancers come from?

probes.a: Right sided growths present with anaemia and a mass because liquid stool passes without obstruction, while left sided annular growths present with constipation and obstruction, and rectal growths with bleeding and tenesmus.
probes.q: Contrast the typical presentation of right sided, left sided and rectal cancer in one sentence each.

probes.a: Mismatch repair testing tells whether the tumour is microsatellite unstable, which predicts poor response to chemotherapy, strong response to checkpoint inhibitors, and a possible hereditary syndrome.
probes.q: Why is every tumour tested for mismatch repair defects?

rubric.text: Describes the adenoma to carcinoma sequence
Contrasts right, left and rectal presentations by stool content and growth shape
Explains universal mismatch repair testing and what it changes

sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: pathology and site-wise features
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Carcinoma of the colon and rectum means adenocarcinoma arising from the large bowel lining, and most cases develop from adenomatous polyps through a stepwise adenoma to carcinoma sequence. Only a minority of adenomas progress, with risk tied to size and histology.

Three molecular routes drive sporadic disease: chromosomal instability with early APC loss followed by KRAS or BRAF changes and late p53 loss, mismatch repair deficiency giving microsatellite instability, and CpG island methylation often in right sided tumours. The routes can overlap in one cancer.
teach.heading: An adenocarcinoma from adenomas

rows: Vague ill health, iron deficiency anaemia, palpable lump; obstruction is late
Annular constricting growth, stool now solid
Increasing constipation needing stronger purgatives, cramps, apple core on imaging
Ulcerated or proliferative growth in a narrow tube
Bleeding with mucus, tenesmus, narrowing of stool calibre

teach.body:
Two facts govern spread and follow up. The liver is the commonest visceral metastatic site: the first distant recurrence in about one third, and involved in over two thirds by death. Yet metastases confined to one site, liver, lung or peritoneum, can still be resected with curative intent.

Every tumour is tested for mismatch repair defects, since microsatellite unstable tumours respond poorly to standard chemotherapy but dramatically to checkpoint inhibitors, and the result also flags possible hereditary disease.
teach.heading: Spread, testing and what is curable

skill.reasoning.colorectal.basics.title: What carcinoma of the colon and rectum is
skill.reasoning.colorectal.basics.why: Right sided, left sided and rectal cancers look like different diseases at the bedside, yet students meet them under one name. Fixing the site first, before any symptom is listed, is what makes every later finding fall into place.

skill.reasoning.colorectal.signs.oneLine: Anaemia or obstruction or tenesmus, and the finger that settles which
pitfalls: Examining the abdomen thoroughly but never performing the rectal examination, which is where ninety percent of rectal cancers are felt.
Calling a loaded descending colon a tumour, when faecal matter pits on pressure and a neoplasm does not.
Missing anaemia because the pallor was never looked for in a patient whose only complaint is bleeding.
Ignoring a hard left supraclavicular node, which hints at distant spread and inoperability.

probes.a: An ulcerated growth with a raised everted edge and indurated base, with distance from the verge, circumference involved, mobility and what the glove shows.
probes.q: What exactly do you record when the finger finds a rectal growth?

probes.a: A right sided growth gives anaemia with a mass and no obstruction, an annular left sided growth gives progressive constipation with a loaded colon, and a rectal growth gives bleeding with mucus and tenesmus.
probes.q: One bedside sentence separates the three sites: give it.

probes.a: Mobility is preserved while the growth stays within the fascia propria of the rectum; fixity to prostate, vagina, bladder, sacrum or sidewall means spread beyond it and usually inoperability.
probes.q: What does a fixed rectal growth tell you anatomically?

rubric.text: Gives the coherent site-wise picture, not a list of symptoms
Describes the malignant rectal findings and what to record
Names the signs of spread that change operability

sources.locator: colorectal_cancer: clinical presentation by tumour site and red flags
Examination of a rectal case: palpation and signs of spread
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
A right sided growth announces itself with anaemia and a lump: liquid stool flows past a fungating mass, which ulcerates and bleeds insidiously while the patient complains only of tiredness, appetite loss and vague discomfort. Obstruction comes late or never.

An annular left sided growth announces itself with constipation: solid stool will not pass a constricting ring, so the patient needs ever stronger purgatives while the colon above loads with faeces that pit on pressure. Cramps and then obstruction follow.
teach.heading: Right anaemia, left obstruction

teach.body:
A rectal growth announces itself with bleeding and disordered emptying: blood mixed with mucus, sometimes passed separately from stool, with a sense of fullness, urgency on rising, and narrowing of the stool stream. Pain is absent at first and arrives late, with spread into pelvic tissue or the sacral plexus.

On the finger, malignancy is an ulcer with a raised everted edge and an indurated base that bleeds readily, or a hard irregular stricture, while a benign stricture feels like a smooth diaphragm with a clean hole. Three quarters sit low in the ampulla and are ulcerative; one quarter sit high and are annular.
teach.heading: Rectal bleeding with a rectal explanation

teach.body:
Spread declares itself in fixed places. A growth fixed to prostate, vagina, bladder, sacrum or pelvic sidewall has left the fascia propria and is usually inoperable. Inguinal nodes matter only for growths at or below the dentate line; iliac nodes hide beyond the hand.

Examine the liver for a hard nodular edge, look for jaundice, nodules and ascites, and never skip the left supraclavicular fossa. Weight loss with cachexia is the systemic signature that the disease has moved beyond the bowel.
teach.heading: Signs that the disease has spread

skill.reasoning.colorectal.signs.title: The colorectal picture at the bedside
skill.reasoning.colorectal.signs.why: Three different pictures share one name, and students who memorise symptoms without the site mix them hopelessly. One mechanism per site, each ending at the finger, turns a long list into three coherent stories.

skill.reasoning.colorectal.differential.oneLine: What else bleeds, blocks or wastes, and the test that excludes each
pitfalls: Labelling rectal bleeding piles in a patient past forty without a rectal examination and sigmoidoscopy.
Calling chronic bloody diarrhoea colitis without excluding cancer, when cancer and colitis share bleeding, mucus and tenesmus.
Treating iron deficiency anaemia with iron alone in an adult without examining the whole large bowel.
Forgetting abdominal tuberculosis in an Indian patient with a mass, altered habit and weight loss.

probes.a: Haemorrhoids, anal fissure, diverticular disease, ulcerative colitis and Crohn disease, colorectal polyps, irritable bowel syndrome, and abdominal tuberculosis.
probes.q: Name six differentials for rectal bleeding with altered bowel habit.

probes.a: Piles bleed painlessly with bright blood splashing separately from stool and never cause weight loss or anaemia of this depth; cancer bleeds with mucus, alters habit and wastes, and is felt on the finger.
probes.q: How do you separate piles from rectal cancer at the bedside?

probes.a: No: cancer and colitis coexist in the differential and in the patient, since longstanding colitis is itself a risk factor. Colonoscopy with segmental biopsies maps both, and a stricture in colitis is cancer until histology says otherwise.
probes.q: Bloody diarrhoea with tenesmus proves colitis, so cancer is excluded. True or false, and why?

rubric.text: Spans benign anal, diverticular, inflammatory, polyp, functional and infective causes
States the rule: never piles without rectal examination and sigmoidoscopy
Names the test that separates each differential

sources.locator: Rectal bleeding: differential diagnosis of benign and malignant causes
sources.source: Browse's Introduction to the Symptoms and Signs of Surgical Disease

teach.body:
Benign anal disease is the commonest mimic and the commonest trap. Internal piles bleed painlessly with bright blood that splashes or streaks the surface of hard stool, without habit change, mucus, weight loss or a palpable growth. A fissure adds sharp cutting pain during and after defecation with a sentinel pile.

The rule never bends: rectal bleeding or altered habit in an adult demands a digital examination and sigmoidoscopy even when piles are staring at you, because piles and cancer happily coexist.
teach.heading: Piles and fissure: common, and never the whole answer

rows: Younger patient, chronic bloody diarrhoea, anal tags or perianal sepsis; yet colitis is also a cancer risk
Left sided pain with fever, saw tooth narrowing; bleeding usually settles
Contrast enema or colonoscopy after inflammation cools
Soft grape-like lesion slipping under the finger, no induration
Pain eased by defecation, no bleeding, no weight loss, normal examination
Clinical criteria once red flags are excluded

teach.body:
In India, abdominal tuberculosis earns its place: a right sided mass with altered habit, weight loss and evening fever can mimic a caecal growth closely, and enlarged nodes with ascites point across. Histology and the full clinical picture decide, not assumption.

Malignant mimics close the list: a loaded colon above an annular lesion is faeces, not tumour, and intestinal obstruction from any cause needs the growth looked for, not assumed absent. Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in any adult mandates visualising the entire large bowel.
teach.heading: Tuberculosis, obstruction and anaemia

skill.reasoning.colorectal.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.reasoning.colorectal.differential.why: Almost every differential here shares one symptom with cancer, which is why single-symptom reasoning keeps missing it. Organising mimics by what proves each one wrong turns a long list into a workup.

skill.reasoning.colorectal.summary.oneLine: Tempo, site, rectal findings and stage in three sentences
pitfalls: Summarising without the site, leaving the listener unable to picture the disease or plan the operation.
Omitting the rectal specifics, so distance, fixity and the glove finding never reach the consultant.
Stating cancer without the stage, fitness and what is still missing, which is where the plan actually lives.

probes.a: The patient with relevant risks, the tempo in months, the syndrome in abstract terms with the site, and the stage with fitness and pending tests.
probes.q: What elements belong in a colorectal summary?

probes.a: Distance from the verge decides sphincter saving, circumference and fixity decide resectability, and the glove finding corroborates bleeding: without them no operative plan can be made.
probes.q: Why does the summary carry the full rectal description?

rubric.text: States tempo in months with the site of disease
Includes distance, extent, edge and fixity with glove finding
Ends with stage, fitness and what is still pending

sources.locator: colorectal_cancer: clinical presentation by tumour site
Carcinoma of the rectum: clinical assessment
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Name the patient with the risks that matter: age past middle life, anaemia, family or polyp history. Then state the tempo: months of bleeding with habit change separates cancer from acute bowel illness and chronic functional pain alike.

Then state the syndrome in abstract terms with the site: altered bowel habit with painless mucus bleeding and tenesmus from a lower rectal growth, or anaemia with a right iliac mass, or progressive constipation with a loaded colon.
teach.heading: Three sentences that contain the case

teach.body:
A 58 year old farmer presents with five months of mucus bleeding per rectum, narrowing stool and incomplete emptying, with 6 kg weight loss. Examination shows pallor with an ulcerated anterior rectal growth 4 cm from the verge involving half the circumference, mobile, bleeding on touch, glove stained with blood and mucus, no nodes, no liver edge.

This is carcinoma of the lower rectum, provisionally resectable, with iron deficiency anaemia, pending biopsy, pelvic MRI and contrast staging for nodes and distant spread.
teach.heading: A worked example

skill.reasoning.colorectal.summary.title: The clinical summary
skill.reasoning.colorectal.summary.why: A colorectal summary without the site and the finger findings is a story without an ending: the listener cannot stage, cannot plan, and cannot tell what is still missing.

skill.investigation.colorectal.workup.oneLine: See the whole colon, prove it under the microscope, map the spread
pitfalls: Stopping at a sigmoidoscopy that shows piles while a synchronous cancer sits higher in unexamined colon.
Trusting a negative stool blood test to exclude cancer, when half of proven cancers test negative from intermittent bleeding.
Starting treatment before mismatch repair status is known, losing the chance of checkpoint cure in rectal disease.
Ordering a PET scan upfront instead of contrast CT and pelvic MRI, which stage cheaper and better.

probes.a: Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel with biopsy, because it finds the cancer, synchronous polyps and second cancers in one sitting.
probes.q: What is the gold standard test when colorectal cancer is suspected, and why?

probes.a: No: about half of proven cancers have a negative stool blood test from intermittent bleeding, while most positive tests in well people show no neoplasm. A negative test never excludes cancer; a positive one needs colonoscopy.
probes.q: A negative stool blood test excludes cancer. True or false, and why?

probes.a: Contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis for distant spread, pelvic MRI for a rectal primary to define the mesorectal margin and nodes, CEA as the baseline for prognosis and follow up, and universal mismatch repair testing.
probes.q: Biopsy proves adenocarcinoma. What completes staging before the MDT meets?

rubric.text: Insists on examining the entire large bowel, not the rectum alone
States the limits of stool blood testing in both directions
Orders the staging set: CT, pelvic MRI for rectal disease, CEA, mismatch repair

sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: investigations and preoperative assessment
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel with biopsy is the gold standard: it finds the cancer, takes the tissue that proves it, and detects the synchronous polyps and second cancers that change the operation. Flexible sigmoidoscopy alone misses proximal disease, and about one and a half percent of normal sigmoidoscopies hide a high risk proximal polyp or cancer.

Where colonoscopy is unavailable, rigid sigmoidoscopy with biopsy plus double contrast barium enema still maps the colon and shows the constant filling defect of an annular growth. The method bends to resources; the rule does not: the whole colon must be seen.
teach.heading: See the whole colon

teach.body:
Stool blood testing screens populations but never rules out cancer in a symptomatic patient: about half of proven cancers test negative because bleeding is intermittent, while most positive tests in well people lead to no neoplasm. A positive test needs colonoscopy; a negative one needs ignoring when red flags persist.

Bloods grade the patient, not the tumour: full blood count with iron studies for the anaemia that decides fitness and transfusion, renal and liver panels for operability, and serum CEA as the staging baseline, since a preoperative level above 5 ng per mL predicts poorer prognosis.
teach.heading: Blood tests grade the patient

teach.body:
Contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis stages distant spread, with MRI or PET only as CT findings dictate. A rectal primary also needs pelvic MRI, which defines the mesorectal margin and nodal status that decide neoadjuvant treatment and the plane of surgery.

Universal mismatch repair or microsatellite testing on the tumour comes before treatment starts: unstable tumours respond poorly to standard chemotherapy but dramatically to checkpoint inhibitors, and the result flags hereditary disease. Chest film excludes lung deposits where CT is out of reach.
teach.heading: Map the spread before treating

skill.investigation.colorectal.workup.title: Confirming and staging the disease
skill.investigation.colorectal.workup.why: Investigations here answer three separate questions: is it cancer, where else has it gone, and what treatment will it answer to. Mixing up which test answers which is how patients get operated without staging or staged without tissue.

skill.reasoning.colorectal.diagnosis.oneLine: Name the site, the TNM and the fitness in one statement
pitfalls: Staging clinically before resection and pathology, when true stage needs the resected specimen and its nodes.
Calling a single liver lesion inoperable without an MDT, when isolated single site metastases are considered curable.
Judging prognosis by tumour size, which carries no weight once nodes and grade are accounted for.
Stating the diagnosis without fitness and anaemia, leaving the plan half made.

probes.a: Depth of wall penetration, regional node involvement, and distant metastasis: T for T1 to T4, N for N1 with one to three nodes and N2 with four or more, M for M1 distant spread.
probes.q: What do T, N and M each measure?

probes.a: Stage IIIB: T3 or T4 with N1 disease and no distant spread. At least twelve nodes must be sampled to call the N honestly.
probes.q: A rectal growth through the muscle coat with two positive mesorectal nodes and clear scans. Stage it, with the pathology condition.

probes.a: Penetration into pericolic fat, poor differentiation, perforation or adherence, venous invasion, CEA above 5, BRAF mutation and right sided site worsen outlook, while microsatellite unstable tumours do better; most recurrences arrive within five years.
probes.q: Beyond TNM, what features worsen or improve prognosis?

rubric.text: Defines T, N and M with the node cutoffs
Stages a case with the twelve node condition
Names modifiers of prognosis beyond TNM

sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: staging and prognosis
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

teach.body:
T measures depth of wall penetration: T1 into submucosa, T2 into muscle, T3 through muscle, T4 into adjacent structures. N counts regional nodes: N1 is one to three, N2 is four or more. M records distant metastasis.

Stages follow: stage I is T1 or T2 with clean nodes, stage II is T3 or T4 with clean nodes, stage III is any T with positive nodes, stage IV is any distant spread. Cure exceeds ninety percent in stage I and falls below five percent with distant colonic spread.
teach.heading: TNM in one grid

teach.body:
Two pathology rules underpin every stage. At least twelve nodes must be sampled, or an N0 is a guess, not a stage. And stage cannot be fixed accurately before resection and microscopic analysis unless gross metastases are already visible.

A complete diagnostic statement therefore names the site, the clinical TNM with its evidence, fitness and anaemia, and what is still missing: carcinoma of the lower rectum, clinically T3N1M0, stage IIIB, with iron deficiency anaemia, pending pathology after resection.
teach.heading: What makes a stage honest

skill.reasoning.colorectal.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and staging logic
skill.reasoning.colorectal.diagnosis.why: A diagnosis of cancer without a stage is a noun without a plan: the stage decides neoadjuvant treatment, the operation, adjuvant treatment and follow up. TNM is the grammar that statement is written in.

skill.annex.colorectal.staging.oneLine: Stage, TNM rule and outlook on one grid
pitfalls: Memorising survival figures without the node count that stages honestly.
Mixing Dukes with TNM in one statement, so nobody knows which system is meant.
Forgetting that nodal disease, not size, drives adjuvant decisions.

probes.a: Stage IIB: T4 with clean nodes. T4 outranks size; nodes decide the numeral.
probes.q: Growth into an adjacent structure, nodes clean, no distant spread. Stage?

probes.a: Any T with N1 or N2 and no distant spread is stage III, and node positivity is what brings adjuvant chemotherapy into the plan.
probes.q: What single finding moves localised disease into stage III, and what does that change?

rubric.text: Places any TNM on the grid correctly

sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: Dukes and TNM staging
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery

rows: Cured by complete resection in over nine in ten
High risk features may still need adjuvant treatment
Any T, N1 or N2, M0
Distant spread; single site deposits may still resect

teach.body:
Read depth first, nodes second, spread last: a T4 with clean nodes is stage II, while a small T1 with one positive node is stage III. Nodal status outweighs size every time, and size alone never stages.

About nine in ten localised cases survive five years, roughly three quarters with regional spread, and well under one in five with distant spread. The older Dukes system maps alongside: A within the wall, B through it, C nodes involved, D distant spread.
teach.heading: How to use this grid

teach.body:
Every resection specimen must report the checklist that stages honestly: depth of penetration, grade, venous and perineural invasion, margin status, mismatch repair result, and the node count with at least twelve sampled.

Poor outlook flags travel with the report: penetration into pericolic fat, poor differentiation, perforation or adherence to neighbours, venous invasion, preoperative CEA above 5, BRAF mutation, and a right sided primary. Microsatellite unstable tumours carry a better prognosis.
teach.heading: The pathology checklist

skill.annex.colorectal.staging.title: TNM staging grid for colorectal cancer
skill.annex.colorectal.staging.why: Staging questions are asked from this grid and treatment flows from it, so a student who can place any finding here can answer both the viva and the bedside.

skill.treatment.colorectal.management.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of modality and principle. Specific agents, routes, combinations and schedules must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline and local protocols at the time of prescribing. CliniX does not prescribe.
skill.treatment.colorectal.management.oneLine: Resect what is local, shrink what is rectal, follow everything
pitfalls: Operating on a rectal cancer without pelvic MRI, then discovering an involved margin that neoadjuvant treatment could have cleared.
Starting chemotherapy before mismatch repair status returns, closing the door on checkpoint cure in unstable disease.
Forgetting surveillance after curative resection, when most recurrences arrive within five years and CEA rises first.
Leaving the family unscreened when a hereditary pattern stares from the history.

probes.a: Surgical resection with regional lymphadenectomy is the curative mainstay for localised colon and rectal cancer, through the colorectal multidisciplinary team.
probes.q: What is the curative mainstay for localised disease?

probes.a: Total neoadjuvant therapy with chemotherapy and chemoradiation before surgery, to downstage, clear the mesorectal margin and preserve the sphincter where possible.
probes.q: A T3 node positive low rectal cancer: what comes before the knife, and why?

probes.a: Adjuvant oxaliplatin based chemotherapy such as FOLFOX or CAPOX for stage III and high risk stage II; metastatic disease gets systemic chemotherapy with targeted antibodies by RAS and mismatch status; isolated single site deposits are resected with curative intent.
probes.q: Who gets adjuvant treatment, and how is metastatic disease approached?

rubric.text: States resection with lymphadenectomy as the curative mainstay
Gives neoadjuvant therapy for locally advanced rectal disease
Describes surveillance and family screening

sources.locator: Carcinoma of the colon and rectum: surgical and adjuvant treatment
sources.source: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery
NICE guideline: Suspected cancer recognition and referral

teach.body:
Localised colon cancer is cured by resection with regional lymphadenectomy, planned for clear margins with at least twelve nodes for staging. Rectal cancer follows the same principle through sphincter sparing low anterior resection where the complex is free, or abdominoperineal resection with a permanent stoma where it is not.

Locally advanced rectal disease, T3 or T4 or node positive, is downstaged first with total neoadjuvant therapy: chemotherapy with chemoradiation before surgery. Obstruction or perforation presents as an emergency and goes to the operating theatre by MDT decision, not by routine pathway.
teach.heading: Surgery first, or shrinkage first

teach.body:
After resection, stage III and high risk stage II disease receive adjuvant oxaliplatin based chemotherapy such as FOLFOX or CAPOX. Metastatic disease is treated systemically: cytotoxic chemotherapy with targeted antibodies, anti EGFR agents only in RAS wild type tumours and the anti VEGF antibody bevacizumab.

Mismatch repair deficient, microsatellite unstable tumours receive checkpoint inhibitors, and unstable rectal cancers may be cured by these drugs alone without surgery, radiation or chemotherapy. That is why treatment waits for the mismatch result.
teach.heading: Drugs around the operation

teach.body:
Surveillance after curative resection catches the recurrences that cluster within five years: CEA every three months for two years then six monthly to five years, colonoscopy at one year then three yearly then five yearly, with cross sectional imaging for stage II and III disease.

In Indian practice, refer early to the medical college colorectal MDT with biopsy and scans in hand; operative, chemo and radiation costs are covered for eligible families under schemes such as Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, and first degree relatives of hereditary or young onset cases need colonoscopic screening.
teach.heading: Follow up, referral and the family

skill.treatment.colorectal.management.title: Managing colorectal cancer
skill.treatment.colorectal.management.why: The operation cures only when the staging, the neoadjuvant decision and the follow up around it are all correct. Management here is a sequence owned by a team, not a single procedure to memorise.

stations.title: Take a history and plan staging

cases.fallback: I do not understand, doctor. Can you ask that in a simpler way?

abdominal_pain_cramps.reply: There are cramps low down on the left side before motions, and they ease after I pass stool. No vomiting, no swelling of the belly.

cues: how often do you pass stool
bowel_habit_change.reply: Earlier I passed once daily without trouble. Now I go three or four times, mostly mucus and small amounts, and the motions have become thin like a pipe stem for two months.

comorbidity_medicines.reply: No sugar, no pressure. I take only iron tablets from the health centre for two months. No blood thinners, no painkillers daily.

family_polyposis_history.reply: My elder brother had an operation for intestine cancer at fifty five in the civil hospital. Nobody else. My sons are well.

cues: can you come to the hospital
family_support_plan.reply: My younger son will come with me to Satara or Pune wherever you refer. I cut cane seasonally; my brother will manage the field.

onset_tempo.reply: It started about five months ago with a little blood. It has slowly increased, and the thinning of stool came two months back.

past_bowel_polyps.reply: No operation on the bowel ever. No years of loose motions. Once the doctor said piles, but no procedure was done.

presenting.reply: Doctor, for five months blood comes when I pass stool, with sticky mucus, and now the stool has become thin. I feel the bowel never empties fully.

prior_bowel_tests.reply: Only a stool test at the health centre which showed blood, and blood tests showing less blood. No scope or X-ray of the intestines yet.

rectal_bleeding_detail.reply: Dark red blood mixed with sticky mucus coats the stool, and sometimes only blood and mucus come without stool. It is painless. The pan water turns red.

stool_blood_relation.reply: Mostly the blood coats the outside and mixes with mucus. Twice only mucus and blood came with a strong urge but no stool. Paper alone is never the story.

cues: feeling of fullness in the rectum
tenesmus_evacuation.reply: Yes, I feel something sits inside and the bowel never empties. Early morning the urge wakes me and only mucus comes. That is the most troubling part.

tobacco_diet_habits.reply: I chew tobacco since twenty years and smoke bidis occasionally. Food is bhakri, dal, little vegetables. Meat rarely, festival only.

cues: pain in the hips or back
urinary_pressure_symptoms.reply: Urine passes normally, no burning, no stoppage. No back or hip pain shooting down the legs. No leg swelling.

weight_appetite_loss.reply: I have lost about 6 kg, clothes hang loose. Appetite is less and I tire in the field by afternoon. My wife says my face looks pale.

cases.opening: Shankar Jadhav, 58, has been sent from the rural health centre with five months of bleeding per rectum. He sits with a cloth bag of old prescriptions, answering slowly, his son beside him. Introduce yourself and take a history.

patient.name: Shankar Jadhav
patient.residence: Rural, lives with his wife and two sons

cases.title: A cane cutter with five months of bleeding and narrowing stool

diagnosis.answer: Carcinoma of the lower rectum, clinically mobile, T3N1M0, stage IIIB, with iron deficiency anaemia.

differentialModel.answer: Ulcerated carcinoma of the lower rectum with mesorectal nodes. Consider haemorrhoids with a second lesion, diverticular disease, ulcerative colitis, a benign adenomatous polyp, anal fissure, and abdominal tuberculosis.

skill.exam.surg.dre_surgical.finding: Ulcerated growth on the anterior rectal wall, lower edge 4 cm from the anal verge, involving half the circumference, with a raised everted edge and indurated base. Mobile on the muscular layer, bleeds readily on touch. Prostate normal behind the growth. Glove stained with dark blood and mucus.

skill.exam.surg.lump_inspection_palpatio.finding: Abdomen soft, no discrete lump and no guarding. Descending colon loaded with faeces that pits on pressure. Liver edge not palpable, no ascites, no visible peristalsis. Hernial sites free.

skill.exam.surg.perianal_inspection.finding: Perianal skin stained with blood mixed mucus with mild excoriation. No prolapsed piles, no sentinel pile, no fistula opening, no condyloma. Anal tone normal on parting the margins.

skill.exam.surg.proctoscopy.finding: Friable ulcerated proliferative mass seen on the anterior wall, bleeding on contact of the scope. Mucosa above the growth normal as far as seen. No internal piles prolapsing. Punch biopsy taken from the edge, haemostasis secured.

skill.exam.surg.regional_nodes.finding: No inguinal nodes palpable on either side. No left supraclavicular node. Axillae free.

skill.gen.appearance.finding: Thin built man looking his age, pale conjunctiva and tongue, mild weight loss. No jaundice, no clubbing, no leg swelling. Alert and cooperative.

skill.gen.edema.finding: No pedal oedema on either side.

skill.gen.vitals.finding: Pulse 96 regular, low volume. Blood pressure 118/74. Respiratory rate 18. SpO2 98 percent on room air. Afebrile. Pallor explains the tachycardia; no postural symptoms volunteered.

cect_cap.label: Contrast CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis
cect_cap.note: Completes distant staging once the rectal primary is proven: lungs and liver are the organs that change stage IV.
cect_cap.result: No liver lesions. No lung nodules. No para-aortic nodes. Kidneys excrete normally.

cea.label: Serum carcinoembryonic antigen
cea.note: Baseline for prognosis and follow up: a raised level predicts poorer outlook and its fall and rise tracks treatment and recurrence.
cea.result: 18 ng per mL, raised above the 5 ng per mL threshold that predicts poorer prognosis.

colonoscopy_biopsy.label: Colonoscopy with biopsy
colonoscopy_biopsy.note: Mandatory and diagnostic: only histology proves adenocarcinoma, and only the whole colon excludes a synchronous second lesion.
colonoscopy_biopsy.result: Ulcerated circumferential growth in the lower rectum from 4 cm upward; rest of the colon to the caecum normal with two small polyps removed. Histology: moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma. Mismatch repair testing requested.

fbc_iron.label: Full blood count with iron studies
fbc_iron.note: Grades the anaemia that decides fitness for bowel preparation and major resection, and sets iron replacement and transfusion cover.
fbc_iron.result: Haemoglobin 8.6 g per dL. Microcytic hypochromic picture. Ferritin low, fitting iron deficiency from chronic blood loss.

liver_usg_lft.label: Liver ultrasound with liver function tests
liver_usg_lft.note: Bedside available cross check for liver deposits and fitness where contrast CT is delayed or unaffordable.
liver_usg_lft.result: Liver normal in size and echo texture, no focal lesion. Bilirubin and transaminases within normal limits.

mri_pelvis.label: MRI of the pelvis
mri_pelvis.note: Maps the mesorectal margin and nodes that decide neoadjuvant treatment and the plane of surgery.
mri_pelvis.result: 4 cm anterior rectal mass through the muscle coat into mesorectal fat with a clear mesorectal fascia. Two suspicious mesorectal nodes. Sphincter complex free.

pet_scan.label: PET scan upfront
pet_scan.note: Not indicated as a first step: contrast CT and pelvic MRI already stage this case, and PET is reserved for what CT leaves doubtful.

accept: urgent referral to a colorectal multidisciplinary unit
correction of anaemia with iron and transfusion cover
contrast staging with pelvic MRI for the mesorectal margin
managementModel.answer: Refer urgently to the colorectal unit with biopsy and scans, correct the anaemia, complete mismatch repair testing, give neoadjuvant chemoradiation for T3N1 rectal disease, resect with lymphadenectomy, and enter CEA and colonoscopy surveillance with family screening.

teachingPoints: Tempo in months is the first diagnosis: five months of mucus bleeding with habit change points to rectum, not piles and not acute dysentery.
The glove finding corroborates the story: dark blood with mucus on the finger matches mixed bleeding passed separately from stool.
Distance, circumference and fixity are the examination: 4 cm from the verge, half the wall, mobile, which is what keeps sphincter saving on the table.
A loaded colon that pits is faeces above an annular hold up, not a second tumour; a neoplasm never pits.
Biopsy proves, MRI maps, CT completes: histology names adenocarcinoma while MRI stages the margin and nodes and CT excludes distant spread.
Anaemia travels with stage: haemoglobin 8.6 with a raised CEA sets transfusion cover and prognosis before any knife is lifted.
Referral is treatment: a district diagnosis with biopsy, MRI and mismatch testing in hand, sent early to the colorectal MDT, is what keeps a curable stage curable.
